Digg was the first online community to use up and down votes in a modern way. Older sites like slashdot had a version of it, but Digg was the first crowdsourced news aggregator to do it like this. The model was copied on Reddit and Voat, which is why people are still noticing similarities between Reddit and Voat.

So why did Digg go under while Reddit thrives and Voat explodes with activity?

Digg made a series of mistakes that alienated the userbase, but the final straw happened when Digg implemented the infamous v4 update, which was unpopular enough to drive people to Reddit and other online communities. Digg's founder Kevin Rose said that his biggest regret was trying to go mainstream in order to monetize, rather than spending his energies cultivating the community he already had.

To me, that sounds a little simplistic. Some online community sites like Facebook monetize well, so why wasn't Digg more like Facebook and less like MySpace? What really went wrong? How could they have avoided failure? Is it really monetization that kills communities or is it more nuanced than that? Is it possible to monetize a news aggregation community based on Digg's model without everything falling apart?

I wasn't a member of Digg, but I am familiar with what happened. I was a long-time redditor, so I can explain from my point of view what happened. Sorry this got long, but whatever, it's an opinion

First, when you monetize something, you put yourself somewhat at the mercy of the people paying you. If people are paying you for hosting ads and someone doesn't like what they see on your site, its all to easy for them to go to the company that is advertising and say, "We don't like that you are advertising on a site that holds an opinion that tied my thong in a knot, so we will not use your product as long as you continue to advertise there." If you take a brigade with you, the company might just say, ok, well we cant give you money for ads as long as you allow this opinion to stay on your site. The website now has a choice...Lose money or remove an opinion.

The second reason is that, quite frankly, if you are a user, and aren't paying for a service or product, then the reality is, You are the product. This is prevelant with organizations like Google or Facebook. They mine everything they can about you and sell that info. I won't expose an opinion on this other than to say that I do not choose to be a product so I do not use Facebook.

This leads me to my first gripe with recent changes to Reddit...The Share function. Several months ago, if you were on a decent post, you could select "Share" enter a username and the post would show up in that users reddit inbox. My girlfriend and I spent a lot of time sending stuff back and forth. Then it changed suddenly. Now you can only share with FB, Twitter or by email. Well, I don't use facebook or twitter and I don't want to connect my email to anything, so suddenly, I am not going to be able to use that functionality. Driving traffic through FB and Twitter was a move to monetize users. This is a behavior that limited what I was willing to do, and for me, it was a negative change and the start of the decline of my appreciation for Reddit.

Now, regarding the reason Digg failed. I think it is due to the fact that they got Experts in to develop a system full of cool stuff that the demographics say that the users want. Turns out, not so much. A case could be made that Microsoft did the same thing with Vista. Facebook is smarter about is. They make minor tweaks here and there rather than radical overhauls. People may not LIKE the changes, but they are small and they have time to get used to them or learn to work around them instead of being thrown into an entirely new system.

Finally, there is a very weird (to me) concept called "Driving Traffic". Some preface to this from my point of view... I worked for one of the Big dotCom success/utter failure stories in the late 90's, early 2K's. I worked there from the start up, through the IPO and then the crash. After 2 years of hard work, we had a great site, lots of visitors and an IPO that earned us about $85 Million. Shares opened that day at $9 bucks and closed at $36. A lot of us had a metric fuck-ton of options that quadrupled that day... Yay Us!

A month later, the executive leadership announced that they had just signed a 5 year contract with Yahoo to "Drive Traffic" to our site. That contract cost us $90 million dollars. $90 fucking million dollars. I was new to the industry but I was thinking...How many billboards and advertisements could you buy with $90 million dollars?

Well, the traffic never came to fruition. We were on the hook for the $90 mil, but traffic and our stock prices went into a steady decline. One Quarter, I had enough in stock that I could cash out to pay off my house. I chose to wait hoping to avoid a significant capital gains hit. The very next quarter, Ameritrade billed me $0.25 processing fee for my account, because my portfolio couldn't cover the fee (diversify people, FFS, diversify).

The point is, Traffic can be a revenue stream, but it seems very risky to put all your eggs in that basket. you need to offer something else. I would easily pay a dollar or two to be a member of a site like this. I would rather Pay to use it the way I want to, to be able to say what I want, look at the content I want, and remain uncensored, than to be a product. I think most people get their back up when they realize that they are what is being sold.

LOL, yeah I had the same experience working for Mindspring back in the boom-bust days. That driving traffic stuff is very insightful. I never noticed the share function on Reddit. I wonder how many people used it?

Anyway, as far as paying for a community goes... yeah, I'm with you on that. If voat does not work out my backup plan is to get a usenet account. It's decentralized and paid for by the users. I don't mind paying a few bucks a month for a good community.

People really just want something basic that they can interact on, right? The trick would be giving people a few tools to filter the noise out. IDK, it might be an idea for later.
